evidence_notes: Letter to a senator; claim = the Electoral College should be abolished because it is unfair; two block quotes from the source (winner-take-all/swing states; 2012 toss-up campaigning), each followed by the writer's own commentary extending unfairness from voters to would-be candidates (the Oklahoma hypothetical). org 4 (thesis stated early and held, opening letter frame and closing both present, both body parts relate — but the two quote-plus-comment blocks make the same fairness point and could swap without loss, so rung 5 fails). dev 4 (quoted source material is specific and the connection to the claim is stated after each quote, but the explanation restates rather than interprets, and the quotes sit alongside the writer's sentences rather than inside them, so rung 5 fails). conv 4 (misspellings — Senetor, Collge, opporitunity — are visible and one pronoun reference wrong-foots briefly, but nothing needs repair to get the meaning; sentence shapes vary; rung 5 fails because the reader is occasionally slowed). arg 4 (position clear, committed and held, and one reason is actually reasoned — candidates ignore states they cannot win, therefore non-swing voters and candidates go unheard; the concession 'yes, the toss-up states are more listened to, but' is acknowledged rather than answered, and the conclusion is the one the prompt's framing already implies, so rung 5 fails).

Letter to a senator; claim = replace the Electoral College with the popular vote; Source 1 quoted on each candidate having 'his or her own group of electors' and then unpacked in the writer's own words (voters choose electors, not the president); Source 2 paraphrased loosely on voter confusion; closes on the writer's own coming eligibility to vote. org 4 (controlling idea stated early and held, opening orients and the 'when I turn eighteen' closing does real work, every body part relates — but paragraph 2 restates paragraph 1's direct-voting point and the two source paragraphs could swap, so rung 5 fails). dev 4 (Source 1 quote is specific and the essay states what it means and why that matters, reaching the listed/explained line; paragraph 2 offers no support at all and Source 2 is characterized only loosely, so specificity is not maintained throughout and rung 5 fails). conv 4 (typos — canadate, electios, didnt, 'It make smore sense' — are visible but repairable at a glance; rung 5 fails because sentences run largely to one declarative pattern rather than varying in length and shape). arg 4 (position clear, committed and the writer's own; one reason genuinely reasoned — because electors, not citizens, cast the deciding votes, the citizen's vote is indirect and therefore less fair; no opposing view is engaged and 'the people should be the ones voting' restates the position rather than surfacing a governing principle, so rung 5 fails).

Limiting car usage; opens claiming environmental benefits, then reverses to 'this is America, we like our cars,' announces 'yes, this is off topic,' and ends proposing a cleaner fuel source instead of less driving. Support = Beijing polluted by vehicle emissions; the writer's own Ford Mustang; recession as the real reason young Americans do not buy cars. org 3 (a controlling idea is stated in the opening, but rung 4 fails on 'held' — the position moves from endorsing limits to refusing them, and the closing lands on a different proposal than the one the essay opened with; unity breaks inside the second and third parts). dev 4 (Beijing is a named case and the Mustang a realized personal example, and the connection is stated for both — 'this has negative effects on people's health,' 'that is the problem, people will not want to give up driving'; rung 5 fails because the recession and noise-pollution claims are asserted with no support and the explanations restate rather than add). conv 4 (spelling and punctuation slips — Bejing, reallty, relenquished, 'of of', semicolon splices — are visible and 'it will not be relenquished by all' is approximate word choice, but sentence lengths and shapes genuinely vary and nothing has to be repaired; rung 5 fails on the accumulating slips). arg 4 (position is the writer's own and committed even where it drifts, and one reason is actually reasoned — people cannot afford car, insurance and fuel, therefore declining car ownership is economic rather than environmental; rung 5 fails because the acknowledged opposing point 'it is true that driving less will protect our environment' is answered only by an unargued assertion about what people will do).

Driverless cars; essentially a report of the source — Google and General Motors developing self-driving cars, smart roads abandoned as too costly an upgrade, cameras and sensors locating the car, current cars still needing an alert driver for road work — with the opening question 'but will you let them?' never answered. org 3 (a controlling idea is stated — driverless cars still cannot fully drive themselves — but rung 4 fails on the frame: there is no closing, the essay stops on a stray aside about outrunning the authorities). dev 3 (Google, GM, cameras and sensors, road work are specific, so rung 3 passes, but rung 4 fails — the source material is listed in the order the source presents it and the reader supplies the connection to any claim; the phrasing is lightly stitched from the source, which caps the trait here). conv 3 (pervasive misspelling — thear, whear, requir, abble, currnt, objstical, genration, authortys — makes the reader re-read to repair sentences such as 'still require a drive to be alert,' but meaning is recoverable throughout and never has to be guessed, so rung 3 passes and rung 4 fails). arg 2 (rung 2 passes on the summary claim that current cars still need drivers, but rung 3 fails — the essay poses the issue as a question and never commits to a point of view on it; the one evaluative remark, that a generation unable to drive 'could be a good thing' for evading authorities, is a throwaway that barely engages the issue).

Face on Mars; claim = the structure is a natural landform; support = the 1976, 1998 and 2001 photographs of successively better quality, comparison to terrestrial mesas and buttes, and the inference that a camera able to resolve shacks or pyramids would certainly resolve a giant face. org 4 (thesis first sentence, held, opening orients and the closing lands the claim, and every body part relates to it — but paragraph 2 largely re-narrates paragraph 1's camera chronology and could swap with paragraph 3, so rung 5 fails). dev 4 (dated photographs, NASA, mesa/butte are specific and the connection is stated — better cameras yielded the conclusion, and 'if you could see small structures on Mars, then you could see a giant human face'; rung 5 fails because the Hollywood-films aside and the mesa/butte comparison are dropped unexplained and 'it could of been created by Martians' contradicts the claim it sits under). conv 3 (errors accumulate — could of, Simlar, naturaly, quailty, Hollywoof, 'scientists also include to support their statement,' and the truncated 'seen in the American' — and the reader re-reads to repair these, though meaning stays recoverable, so rung 3 passes and rung 4 fails). arg 4 (clear committed position held throughout, and one reason is genuinely reasoned — resolution good enough to show small artificial structures rules out an unnoticed artificial face; rung 5 fails because the believers in Martians are mentioned but never answered and the conclusion is exactly what the prompt's framing implies).

Against self-driving cars; claim = they are dangerous, irresponsible and corrosive of human connection; moves from general over-reliance on technology, to a concession that electronics have helped but are human-operated, to teen inexperience and accident risk, to the closing claim that the cars will end the everyday bonding that happens inside them. org 5 (controlling idea early and held, opening and closing both do work and the closing lands somewhere the opening did not — the social cost rather than the safety cost; no pair of body parts swaps without loss, since 'now don't get me wrong' depends on the preceding paragraph and 'not only... but' depends on the safety paragraph; rung 6 fails because the general technology-dependence opening sits loosely outside the controlling idea and the sequence's move is not cleanly nameable throughout). dev 3 (rung 3 passes on the teen-accident claim and the realized in-car bonding scene, but rung 4 fails — the claims about accidents, cost of technology and social loss are asserted and the reader supplies the connection from each to the position; almost all support is general). conv 4 (genuine sentence variety — rhetorical questions, short punches, longer builds — with occasional slips: figuritevly, woudln't, accidnets, the garbled 'travel is as good as that as well,' and 'descendent of humanity' for descent; errors are visible but do not accumulate, so rung 4 holds and rung 5 fails on the approximate word choices). arg 5 (position clear and held; reasons are reasoned rather than asserted — machines lacking a rational mindset should not be given the operating role, teens who never learn the basics compound the group already most prone to accidents; the opposing consideration that technology has genuinely improved life is acknowledged and answered by a stated distinction — those inventions still depend on a human to operate them; and the essay reaches a conclusion the prompt's framing does not imply, the erosion of human contact. rung 6 fails: the strongest objection, that autonomous cars may be safer than human drivers, is never met).

Against driverless cars; claim = they should not be allowed because they are unsafe and encourage laziness; quotes the article on sensors and on cars notifying drivers when work zones require human skills, plus the hypothetical of a driver asleep as a work zone approaches. org 4 (thesis stated early in its own sentence and held, opening names the article and the closing restates the judgment, and both body parts relate to the controlling idea — but the two are freely interchangeable and the laziness paragraph wanders into praising the sensors and smart-road ideas before returning, so rung 5 fails). dev 4 (the sensors quote is praised in a paragraph arguing there is no point and so is discarded as not bearing on its claim; what remains — the work-zone quote — is specific and the connection is stated, 'if you still have to do all of that then what is the point of having a driverless car,' extended by the sleeping-driver scenario, so rung 4 passes; rung 5 fails because the laziness claim is supported only circularly and the alternatives offered are general). conv 2 (rung 2 passes, meaning is broadly recoverable, but rung 3 fails — 'then thats way they have buses for that way they have trines' and 'then ther a big thing' force the reader to guess at intended structure rather than repair it, and dropped and garbled words are frequent throughout). arg 4 (position stated with commitment and held, and one reason is genuinely reasoned — if the driver must still handle work zones, the purported benefit of the car is defeated; rung 5 fails because the good ideas conceded from the article are mentioned and dismissed rather than answered, and the conclusion goes no further than the prompt implies).

Against the Facial Action Coding System; claim = it is a useless, invasive waste of money; support = the text's step-by-step instructions for a happy expression, contrasted with everyday recognition of happiness and anger, plus repeated assertions about taxes and how few people would use it. org 3 (a controlling idea is stated in the first sentence and held and the parts all relate, but rung 4 fails on the repetition test — the fourth part restates the money objection already made in the first and third parts without adding to it, and the closing dissolves into a run of rhetorical questions that stops rather than closes). dev 3 (rung 3 passes marginally on the reference to the text's step-by-step expression instructions, but rung 4 fails as a whole: the money, privacy and low-uptake claims are unsupported, much of what is offered as support restates the claim it supports — 'I am going to argue why this is a bad idea, because it is' — and the reader supplies the connection). conv 3 (word choice is generally right and errors are few — whoe, usless, speding — but comma splices and run-ons accumulate, notably the long 'for example in the text... I don't need a machine to tell me how to do that,' and the reader re-reads to repair them; rung 3 passes, rung 4 fails). arg 4 (position clear, committed and held, and one reason is genuinely reasoned — the capacity being coded is one people already exercise unaided, so the machine is redundant; rung 5 fails because no benefit of the system is ever acknowledged, let alone answered, no governing principle is made explicit, and the essay circles back to its opening judgment rather than reaching past the prompt's framing).

Seagoing cowboys; opens with a fragment naming Luke's persuasive purpose, narrates his post-graduation jobs and his friend's invitation, then gives the 1945 context of ruined countries and 44 nations joining to supply food and animals, closing on why the reader should join. org 3 (a controlling idea is recoverable and stated in the essay's own words in the closing, so rung 3 passes, but rung 4 fails — the opening fragment gives no orientation and the paragraph on working two part-time jobs to buy his own things does not relate to convincing anyone to participate). dev 3 (1945 and the figure of 44 nations are specific and the historical context is connected to Luke's signing up, but the historical sentences reproduce the source's phrasing lightly stitched together, which caps the trait here; the closing reason is circular — giving is nice because giving is nice). conv 2 (rung 2 passes, the gist is recoverable, but rung 3 fails — 'all they supplies they need' and the sixty-word closing run-on with a missing subject, 'beacuse wants you to learn how to help other,' force the reader to guess at intended structure and referents rather than repair them). arg 2 (rung 2 passes — a position that others should join is stated — but rung 3 fails: the opening is the prompt's own wording handed back as a fragment, the body is narrative summary in which the writer never commits to a view, and the closing reasons restate the position rather than adding commitment).

Venus source analysis; controlling statement = the author suggests studying Venus is a worthy pursuit despite the dangers; body assembles quoted evidence of danger — limited insight from orbit because light cannot penetrate the atmosphere, 170 degrees at altitude, no spacecraft surviving more than a few hours, 97 percent carbon dioxide and 800-degree surface — before quoting the author's closing justification. org 4 (controlling idea stated first, held, restated in a closing that adds the author's justification, and every body part relates to the 'despite the dangers' half — but the three danger paragraphs are a pile of interchangeable quotations that could swap freely, so rung 5 fails). dev 4 (quotations are specific, with figures throughout, and the connection is stated for several — 'the wind and atmosphere are both something us humans would not be able to handle,' 'a human in that hot temperature would fry'; rung 5 fails because the paragraph-six quotation is dropped without any comment and the commentary elsewhere restates the quotation rather than adding to it, with the borrowed material sitting alongside the writer's sentences rather than inside them). conv 3 (in the writer's own sentences errors accumulate — comma splices, 'the wind and atmosphere and both something,' Regaurdless, extreamly, 'reguardless of what it is aboutl' — forcing re-reading to repair, and the quote-introduction formula repeats one pattern; meaning never has to be guessed, so rung 3 passes and rung 4 fails). arg 3 (the position is clear and held and a little commitment is added in the writer's own voice — 'the conditions of this planet are just not living conditions,' 'as the reader, we want to know more' — so rung 3 passes; rung 4 fails because no reason is actually reasoned: the essay documents the dangers but never says why they fail to defeat the pursuit, and the closing restates the opening in the prompt's own words).
